title: NRI Deposit Inflows Surge Seven-Fold to $36.24 Billion on RBI Swap Push
excerpt: FCNR(B) dollar deposits drew $34.53 billion — 95% of all inflows — in April-July FY27 after the RBI's concessional swap facility let banks offer NRIs dollar rates with no currency risk; total NRI deposits crossed $200 billion.
body:
• Net inflows into NRI deposit schemes surged 678.2% year-on-year to $36.24 billion during April-July FY27, up from $4.66 billion in the same period of FY26, according to RBI data released in the central bank's September bulletin.
  • FCNR(B) dollar deposits drove the spike, drawing $34.53 billion — about 95% of all inflows — versus $772 million a year earlier, after the RBI's June 8 concessional swap facility let banks offer NRIs dollar deposit rates with no currency risk.
  • Rupee-denominated NRE inflows collapsed 91% to $207 million from $2.42 billion, while NRO deposits held steady at $1.51 billion; total outstanding NRI deposits crossed $200 billion, reaching $200.89 billion at end-July.
  • Action for NRIs: the special swap window for fresh FCNR(B) deposits closed August 31 — about $133 billion was mobilized through the facility — so advertised dollar deposit rates may be less generous now; the swap channels for banks' external commercial borrowings remain open until December 31.

Inflows into India's non-resident Indian deposit schemes recorded a near seven-fold surge in the first four months of FY27, powered almost entirely by foreign-currency deposits drawn in through a special Reserve Bank of India swap facility. Net NRI deposit inflows jumped 678.2% year-on-year to $36.24 billion during April-July FY27, from $4.66 billion a year earlier, according to RBI data in the central bank's September bulletin.

The surge was driven by foreign currency non-resident (bank), or FCNR(B), deposits. Inflows into FCNR(B) accounts soared to $34.53 billion in the four-month period, compared with just $772 million a year earlier, accounting for roughly 95% of all fresh NRI inflows.

Context & Background

"Inflows into FCNR(B) accounts soared to $34.53 billion in the four-month period, compared with just $772 million a year earlier, accounting for roughly 95% of all fresh NRI inflows."

The catalyst was the RBI's concessional USD-INR swap facility, introduced on June 8, 2026, specifically to attract foreign-currency inflows. Under the scheme, banks could hand dollars raised through fresh FCNR(B) deposits of three years or more — alongside external commercial borrowings and overseas foreign currency borrowings — to the RBI in exchange for rupees at the spot rate, with the central bank absorbing the hedging cost. That let lenders offer depositors rates well above what they could earn on dollar deposits at home, with no exchange-rate risk. For NRIs, it was a rare arbitrage; for banks, rupees came in cheaply.

Demand outran the RBI's own plans. The window was meant to stay open until September 30, but by August 13 banks had already mobilized $52.3 billion of FCNR(B) money, and the central bank moved the closing date forward to August 31, saying it had raised sufficient foreign currency. The RBI's latest figures put FCNR(B) mobilization under the facility at about $133 billion through August 31. For perspective, the 2013 FCNR(B) swap window, launched during the taper tantrum, raised about $34 billion in total — this year's version brought in roughly four times as much.

Impact & Analysis

The dollars arrived at a critical moment. The rupee closed last Friday at 95.80 per dollar, holding just inside the 96 mark traders have been watching for weeks, and the fresh inflows gave the RBI more ammunition to smooth the currency even as Brent crude traded above $105 a barrel and foreign institutional investors kept selling Indian stocks — September FPI outflows have crossed Rs 17,000 crore, taking 2026 outflows above Rs 2.4 lakh crore.

But swapped money is borrowed time. The RBI will have to return the dollars when the swaps mature, most three to five years out, creating a future obligation on its forward book. Every swapped dollar also became rupees on bank balance sheets, forcing the RBI to drain excess liquidity through reverse repos and bond sales; surplus liquidity that stays too high weakens the transmission between the policy rate and actual borrowing costs.

Analysts noted that some NRI deposit renewals across categories may also have been shifted into FCNR(B) accounts, and banks that paid up aggressively for FCNR(B) money will see the interest cost show up in net interest margins over the next few quarters.

Diaspora Angle

This was the diaspora's money doing the heavy lifting for India's external balance. Outstanding FCNR(B) deposits more than doubled to $68.28 billion at end-July 2026 from $33.6 billion a year earlier, and total outstanding NRI deposits climbed to $200.89 billion — up from $167.86 billion in July 2025 and $168.51 billion in June 2026. Meanwhile outward remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme reached $9.37 billion, up 4.7% year-on-year, even as fresh NRE placements dried up — a sign NRIs preferred to keep savings in hard currency rather than convert into rupees.

What's Next

The October bulletin should confirm the scale of the late-August rush, and markets will watch weekly forex reserves data for how much of the new buffer the RBI is willing to spend. The Monetary Policy Committee announces its decision on October 7 with the repo rate at 5.25%, and the swap channels for external commercial borrowings stay open until December 31.

nri_angle: Diaspora savings became the backbone of India's external defense, as NRIs in the Gulf and US funneled $36.24 billion into Indian banks — while steering clear of rupee-denominated accounts.
author: Diaspora Desk
